accroche: The word that made Thomas Kuhn famous, he himself uses in twenty-one different ways.
contenu_vulgarise:
An 18th-century chemist burns a piece of metal and weighs the resulting ash: it is heavier than the starting metal. Within the theoretical framework of the day, that of phlogiston, a substance supposed to escape during combustion, this result makes no sense. It will take Lavoisier, and a complete change of interpretive grid, for the same experiment to stop being an anomaly and become evidence.

## Normal science, science in crisis

In 1962, the historian of science Thomas Kuhn published *The Structure of Scientific Revolutions* and proposed that we stop describing the history of science as a continuous accumulation of discoveries. At the time, the dominant philosophy of science presented scientific knowledge as a rational sequence of facts, each better established than the last. Kuhn, himself trained in physics before turning to the history of science, starts from concrete cases to show that this picture matches no real episode. Most of the time, he says, a scientific community works in “normal science”: it solves puzzles within a shared framework, a paradigm, without calling that framework into question. Anomalies pile up, tolerated, set aside, until a crisis sets in. Then comes a revolution: a new paradigm replaces the old one, not by adding to it, but by changing the very way problems are posed. Kuhn calls this incommensurability: the followers of Ptolemy and those of Copernicus, those of Newtonian mechanics and those of relativity, are not quite discussing the same thing, even when they use the same words.

## What this shifts

The word that made Kuhn famous turned against him. In 1965, at the international colloquium in the philosophy of science held at Bedford College in London, chaired by W. C. Kneale, the linguist and philosopher Margaret Masterman, founder of the Cambridge Language Research Unit, dissects the book in a session chaired by Karl Popper and finds twenty-one different senses of the word “paradigm,” from an entire worldview to a mere textbook example. Published in 1970 in *Criticism and the Growth of Knowledge*, her critique hits home: in the postscript he added to his book in 1969, Kuhn acknowledges the vagueness and proposes two more precise terms to replace it, “disciplinary matrix,” the set of beliefs and techniques shared by a community, and “exemplar,” the concrete cases of problem solving on which it trains. Neither has really caught on. The vague word, for its part, has left the history of science and invaded the vocabulary of business, marketing, and politics, carried by the very ambiguity it was criticized for.

citation.texte: History, if viewed as a repository for more than anecdote or chronology, could produce a decisive transformation in the image of science by which we are now possessed.

carte.punch: The word that made Kuhn famous, he himself uses in twenty-one different ways.
carte.idee: In 1962, Thomas Kuhn describes science as an alternation of normal science and revolutions through paradigm shifts. In 1965, the linguist and philosopher Margaret Masterman counts twenty-one senses of the word “paradigm” in the book itself. Kuhn concedes the point in his 1969 postscript.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: A full presentation of the work and the debates it has stirred.

quiz.question: Why did Margaret Masterman's critique hit Thomas Kuhn particularly hard?
choix: Because it showed that the Copernican revolution had never taken place
Because it demonstrated that normal science did not exist
Because it counted twenty-one different senses of the central word of Kuhn's book, “paradigm”
Because it proved that Lavoisier had plagiarized his phlogiston-believing predecessors
quiz.explication: Masterman does not dispute the Copernican revolution or the existence of normal science, and says nothing of plagiarism by Lavoisier: she shows that the concept carrying Kuhn's whole thesis, the paradigm, is used in twenty-one different ways in the same book, which Kuhn ended up admitting.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Kuhn, what does a scientific community do during a period of “normal science”?
choix: It solves puzzles within a shared paradigm, without calling that framework into question
It actively seeks to replace the prevailing paradigm with another
It accumulates new facts without ever referring to a theoretical framework
It waits for the next revolution before publishing its results
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Kuhn describes normal science as puzzle solving within an accepted paradigm, without questioning the framework itself, until anomalies pile up.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the term “incommensurability” designate in Kuhn?
choix: The impossibility of measuring the speed at which a scientific revolution occurs
The fact that an old paradigm and a new one can never coexist in the same university
The fact that the followers of two different paradigms are not quite discussing the same thing, even with the same words
Scientists' refusal to accept results obtained by methods foreign to their discipline
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Kuhn calls incommensurability the fact that the followers of two paradigms, Ptolemy and Copernicus for example, are not quite speaking of the same thing even when using the same words.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In his 1969 postscript, what words does Kuhn propose to replace the vague term “paradigm”?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Kuhn proposes “disciplinary matrix,” the set of shared beliefs and techniques, and “exemplar,” the concrete cases of problem solving, but neither has really caught on.
